### Chapter 2
<hr>

# End-to-End Machine Learning Project

<br>
In this chapter you will work through an example project end to end, pretending to be a recently hired data scientist at a real estate company. Here are the main steps you will go through:

1) Get the data
2) Discover and visualise the data to gain insights
3) Prepare the data for Machine Learning algorithms
4) Select a model and train it
5) Fine-tune your model
6) Present your solution
7) Launch, monitor, and maintain your system

## Get the data
Let's get our hands dirty. The data is in`./examples/data/housing.csv`.

```haskell
-- cabal: build-depends: dataframe == 3.1.0.0, text
import qualified DataFrame as D

df <- D.readCsv "./examples/data/housing.csv"

displayMarkdown (D.toMarkdown' (D.take 5 df))
```

```haskell
:set -XTemplateHaskell -XNoOverloadedRecordUpdate
-- Typed column references generated from the CSV header at compile time, so we
-- never write a brittle `F.col @Type "name"` by hand. InferFromSample 300 reads
-- enough rows to see that total_bedrooms has nulls (Maybe Double).
import qualified DataFrame as D
$(D.declareColumnsFromCsvWithOpts (D.defaultReadOptions{D.typeSpec = D.InferFromSample 300}) "./examples/data/housing.csv")
```

Each row represents one district. There are 10 attributes (you can see the first 6 in the screenshot): `longitude`, `latitude`, `housing_median_age`, `total_rooms`, `total_bedrooms`, `population`, `households`, `median_income`, `median_house_value`, and `ocean_proximity`.

The `describeColumns` function is useful to get a quick description of the data. In particular, the total nubmer of tows, each atteibute's type, and the number of nonull values.

```haskell
import DataFrame.Operators

df |> D.describeColumns
   |> D.toMarkdown'
   |> displayMarkdown
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/markdown -->
> | Column Name<br>Text | # Non-null Values<br>Int | # Null Values<br>Int | Type<br>Text |
> | --------------------|--------------------------|----------------------|------------- |
> | total_bedrooms      | 20433                    | 207                  | Maybe Double |
> | ocean_proximity     | 20640                    | 0                    | Text         |
> | median_house_value  | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |
> | median_income       | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |
> | households          | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |
> | population          | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |
> | total_rooms         | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |
> | housing_median_age  | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |
> | latitude            | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |
> | longitude           | 20640                    | 0                    | Double       |

There are 20'640 instances in the dataset, which means that it is fairly small by machine learning standards, but it's eprfect to get started. Notice that the `total_bedrooms` attribute has only 20'433 nonnull values meaning that 207 districts are missing this feature. We will need to take care of this later.

All attrivutes are numerical, except the `ocean_proximity` field. Its type is `Text` which means it is either a unstructured text or a value that we couldn't parse (`Text` is our catchall). When you looked at the first five rows, you probably noticed that the values in the `ocean_proximity` column were repetitive, which means it is probably a categorical attribute. You can find out what categories exist and how many districts belong to each category by using the `valueCounts` function.

```haskell
import Data.Text (Text)

df |> D.valueCounts (D.col @Text "ocean_proximity")
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> [("<1H OCEAN",9136),("INLAND",6551),("ISLAND",5),("NEAR BAY",2290),("NEAR OCEAN",2658)]

Let's look at the other fields. The `summarize` function shows a summary of the numerical attributes.

```haskell
df |> D.summarize
   |> D.toMarkdown'
   |> displayMarkdown
```

The count, mean , min, and max rows are self-explanatory. Note that the null values are ignored (so, for example, the count of total_bedrooms is 20'433 not 20'640). The `StdDev` row shows the standard deviation, which measures how dispersed the values are. The 25t%, median, and 74% rows show the corresponding percentiles: a percentile indicates the value below which a given percentage of observations in a group of observations fall. For example, 25% of the districts have a `housing_median_age` lower than 18, while 50% are lower than 29, and 75% are lower than 37.

Another quick way to get a feel of the type of data you are dealing with is to plot a histogram for each numerical attribute. A histogram shows the number of isntances (on the vertical axis) that have a given value range (o the horizontal axis). You can eithe rplot this one attribute at a time, or you can call the `allHistograms` function on the whole dataset.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame.Display.Web.Plot as Plt

-- the default histograms are messed up, the x axis is
-- not in creating order
allAttributes <- Plt.allHistograms df

displayHtml allAttributes
```

There are a few things you might notice in these histograms:

1) First, the median income attribute does not look like it is expressed in US dillars (USD). After checking with the team that collected the data, you are told this data has been scaled and capped at 15 (actually, 15.0001) for higher median incomes, and at 0.5 (actually 0.4999) for lower median incomes. The numbers represent roughly tens of thousands of dollars (e.g., 3 actually means $30'000). Working with preprocessed attributes is common in machine learning and it is not neccesarily a problem, but you should try ato understand how the data was computed.
2) The housing median age and the median house value were also capped. The latter may be a serious problem since it's your target attribute (your labels). Your machine learning algorithm may learn that prices never go beyond that limit. You need to check with your client team (the team that will use your system's output) to see if this is a problem or not. If they tell you that the need precise predictions even beyond $500'000, the you have two options:

    a) Collect proper labels for the districts whose labels were capped
    b) Remove those districts from the training set (and also from the test set, since your system should not be evaluated poorly if it predicts values beyond $500'000)
3) These attributes have very different scales.
4) Finally, many histograms are tail-heavy: they extend much further to the right of the median than to the left. This may make it a bit harder tfor some Machine Learning algorithms to detect patterns. We will try transforming these attributes later on to have more bell-shaped distributions.

## Create a test set
It may sound strange to voluntarily set aside part of the data at this stage. After all, you have only taken a quick glance at the data, and surely you should learn a whole lot more about it before you decide what algorithms to use, right? This is true but your brain is an amazing pattern detection system, which means that it is highly prone to overfitting: if you look at the test set, you may stumble upon some seemingly interesting pattern in the test data that leads you to select a particular kind of machine learning model. Whe you estimate the generalization error using the test set, your estimate will be too optimistic, and you will launch a system that will not perform as well as expected. This is called _data snooping_ bias.

Creating a test set is theoretically simple: pick some instances randomly, typically 20% of the dataset (or less if your dataset is very large), and set them aside:

```haskell
-- cabal: build-depends: random
import System.Random (mkStdGen, uniformR)
import DataFrame.Operations.Subset (selectRows)

splitTrainTest :: Double -> D.DataFrame -> (D.DataFrame, D.DataFrame)
splitTrainTest r d = let
        shuffled = D.shuffle (mkStdGen 42) d
        testSetSize = round (fromIntegral (D.nRows d) * r) 
    in (D.drop testSetSize d, D.take testSetSize d)

(trainingSet, testingSet) = splitTrainTest 0.2 df

D.dimensions trainingSet
D.dimensions testingSet
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> (16512,10)
> (4128,10)

Well, this works, but it's not perfect. It will break the next time you fetch an updated dataset. To have a stable train/test split even after updating the dataset, a common solution is to use each instances's identifier to decide whether or not it should go in the test set (assuming instances have a unique and immutable identifier). For example, you could compute the hash of each instance's identifier and put that instance in the test set if the hash is lower than or equal to 20% of the maximum hash value. This ensures that the test set will remain conistent across multiple runs even if you refres the dataset. The new test set will contain 20% of the new instances, but it will not contain any instance that was previously in the training set.

Here's a possible implementation:

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import Data.Bits ((.&.))
import Data.Int

testSetCheck :: Int -> Double -> Bool
testSetCheck identifier ratio = fst (uniformR (minBound :: Int64, maxBound) (mkStdGen identifier)) .&. 0xffffffff < (round (ratio * 2 ^ 32))

splitTrainTestById :: Double -> D.Expr Int -> D.DataFrame -> (D.DataFrame, D.DataFrame)
splitTrainTestById ratio ident d = let
        test = (`testSetCheck` ratio) . fromIntegral
    in (D.filter ident (not . test) d, D.filter ident test d)
```

Unfortunately, the housing dataset does not have an identifier column. The simplest solution is to use the row index as the ID:

```haskell
import Data.Bifunctor

-- TODO: mchavinda - Add insertM to monadic API
(trainingSet', testingSet') = df |> D.insert "_id_" [0..(D.nRows df - 1)]
                                 |> splitTrainTestById 0.2 (F.col @Int "_id_")
                                 |> bimap (D.exclude ["_id_"]) (D.exclude ["_id_"])

D.dimensions trainingSet'
D.dimensions testingSet'
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> (16560,10)
> (4080,10)

If you use the row index as a unique identifier, you need to make sure that new data gets appended to the end of the dataset and that no row ever gets deleted. If this is not possible then you can try to use the most stable features to build a unique identifier. For example, a distrct's latitude and longitude are guaranteed to be stable for a few million years, os you could combine them into an ID like so:

```haskell
dfWithId = D.derive @Int "id" (F.lift round (longitude * 1000 + latitude)) df

(trainingSet'', testingSet'') = splitTrainTestById 0.2 (F.col @Int "id") dfWithId

D.dimensions trainingSet''
D.dimensions testingSet''
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> (16152,11)
> (4488,11)

`dataframe` provides the `randomSplit` function that works like `splitTrainTest` out of the box. You can pass it ,ultiple datasets with an identifcal number of rows, and it will split them  ont he same indices (this is very useful, for example, if you have a separate data frame for labels).

```haskell
(test, train) = D.randomSplit (mkStdGen 42) 0.2 df

D.dimensions train
D.dimensions test
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> (16638,10)
> (4002,10)

So far we have considered purely random sampling methods. This is genrally fine if your dataset is large enough (especially relative to the number of attributes), but if it is not, you run the risk of introducing significant sampling bias. When a survery company decides to call 1'000 people to ask them a few questions, they don't just pick 1'000 people randomly in a phone book. They try to ensure that these 100 people are representative of the whole population. For example, the US population is 51.3% females and 48.7% males, so a well-conducted survey in the US would try to maintain this ratio in the sample: 513 female and 487 male. This is called stratified smapling: the populations divided into homogeneous subgroups called strata, and the right number of instances are sampled from each stratum to guarantee that the test set is representative of the overall population. If the people running the survey used purely random sampling, there would be abut a 12% chance of sampling a skewed test set that was either less than 49% male or more than 54% female. Either way, the survey results would be significantly biased.

Suppose you chatted with experts who told you that the median income is a very important attribute to predict median housing prices. You may want to ensure that the test set is representative of the various categories of incomes in the whole dataset. Since the median income is a continuous numerical attribute, you first need to creare an income category attribute. Let's look at hte income histogram more closely: most median incomes go far beyond6. It is important to have a sufficient number of instances in your dataset for each stratum, or else the estimate of a stratum's importance may be biased. This means that you should not have too many strata, and each stratum should be large enough.

```haskell
dfWithIncomeCat = df |> D.derive "income_cat" (
    F.recodeWithCondition 5 [ ((.<=. 1.5), 1)
                            , ((.<=. 3.0), 2)
                            , ((.<=. 4.5), 3)
                            , ((.<=. 6.0), 4)] median_income
  )
  
cats <- Plt.histogram (Plt.mkHistogram "income_cat") dfWithIncomeCat

displayHtml cats
```

Now you are ready to do stratified sampling based on income category.

```haskell
-- TODO: mchavinda - this shouldn't be polymorphic over all columnable it should 
-- only take all Enum
(sTrain, sTest) = D.stratifiedSplit (mkStdGen 42) 0.2 (F.col @Int "income_cat") dfWithIncomeCat

displayMarkdown (D.toMarkdown' (D.summarize (D.select ["median_income"] sTrain)))
displayMarkdown (D.toMarkdown' (D.summarize (D.select ["median_income"] sTest)))
```

You can use the summarize method again to see what the distribution of data is in the test and training sets. As you can see, the test set generated using stratified sampling has income category proportions almost identical to those in the full dataset.

We spent quite a bit of time on test set generation for a good reason: this is an often neglected but critical part of machine learning. Moreover, many of these ideas will be useful when we discuss cross validation. Now it's time to move to the next stage: exploring the data.

## Discover and Visualize the Data to Gain Insights
So far you have only take a quick glance at the data to get a general understanding of the kind of data you are manipulating. Now the goal is to get into a little more depth.

First, make sure you have put the test set aside and you are only exporting the training set. Also if the training set is very large, you may want to sample an exploration set to make manipulations easy and fast. In our case, the set is quite small, so you can must work directly on the full set.

### Visualising geographic data
Since there is geographical information (latitude and longitude), it's a good idea to create a scatterplot of all districts to visualise the data.

```haskell
s <- Plt.scatter (Plt.mkScatter "longitude" "latitude") df

displayHtml s
```

This looks like California all right, but other than that it is hard to see any particular pattern. Setting the alpha option to 0.1 makes it much easier to visualize the places where there is a high density of data points.

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> granite added

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import Granite.Data.Frame
import Granite.Render.Pipeline
import Granite.Spec
import qualified Data.Text as T
import System.Random (mkStdGen)

df' = D.sample (mkStdGen 142) 0.1 df

geoFrame =
    fromColumns
        [ ("lng", ColNum (D.columnAsList longitude df'))
        , ("lat", ColNum (D.columnAsList latitude df'))
        ]

densityLayer =
    (defLayer GeomPoint)
        { layerMapping =
            emptyMapping
                { aesX = Just (ColumnRef "lng")
                , aesY = Just (ColumnRef "lat")
                }
        , layerAesDef = emptyAesDefaults { defSize = Just 2, defAlpha = Just 0.1 }
        }

densityChart =
    emptyChart
        { chartData = geoFrame
        , chartLayers = [densityLayer]
        , chartTitle = Just "District density (alpha = 0.1)"
        , chartSize = SizePixels 760 620
        }

displayHtml (T.unpack (renderChartSvg densityChart))
```

> </svg>

Now let's look at the housing prices. The radius of each circle represents the district's population, and the colour represents the price. We use a colour map ranging from blue (low values) to red (high prices). `Plt.Scatter` only carries `x`, `y`, `colour` and `title`, so for a continuous colour scale plus a size channel we drop down to granite directly.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import Granite.Data.Frame
import Granite.Render.Pipeline
import Granite.Spec
import qualified Data.Text as T

priceFrame =
    fromColumns
        [ ("lng", ColNum (D.columnAsList longitude df'))
        , ("lat", ColNum (D.columnAsList latitude df'))
        , ("value", ColNum (D.columnAsList median_house_value df'))
        , ("pop", ColNum (D.columnAsList population df'))
        ]

priceLayer =
    (defLayer GeomPoint)
        { layerMapping =
            emptyMapping
                { aesX = Just (ColumnRef "lng")
                , aesY = Just (ColumnRef "lat")
                , aesColor = Just (ColumnRef "value")
                , aesSize = Just (ColumnRef "pop")
                }
        , layerAesDef = emptyAesDefaults{defAlpha = Just 0.4}
        }

priceChart =
    emptyChart
        { chartData = priceFrame
        , chartLayers = [priceLayer]
        , chartScales = defScales{scaleColor = Just (SColorContinuous [Hex "#0000ff", Hex "#00ffff", Hex "#ffff00", Hex "#ff0000"])}
        , chartTitle = Just "California housing prices (colour = value, size = population)"
        , chartSize = SizePixels 760 620
        }

displayHtml (T.unpack (renderChartSvg priceChart))
```

This tells you that the housing prices are very much related to location (close to the ocean) and to population density, as you probably knew already. A clustering algorithm should be useful for detecting the main cluster and for adding new features that measure the proximity to the cluster centres. The ocean-proximity attribute may be useful as well, although in Northern California the housing prices in coastal districts are not too high, so it is not a simple rule.

### Looking for correlations
Since the dataset is not too large, you can easily compute the standard correlation coefficient (also called Pearson's r) between every pair of attributes. Let's look at how much each attribute correlates with the median house value:

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import Data.Function (on)
import qualified Data.List as L
import Data.Maybe (fromMaybe)

corrWithValue name = (name, fromMaybe 0 (D.correlation name "median_house_value" df))

correlations = map corrWithValue (D.columnNames df)

mapM_ print (L.sortBy (flip compare `on` snd) correlations)
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> ("median_house_value",1.0)
> ("median_income",0.6880752079585185)
> ("total_rooms",0.13415311380656322)
> ("housing_median_age",0.10562341249320993)
> ("households",6.584265057005642e-2)
> ("total_bedrooms",4.914821959942548e-2)
> ("ocean_proximity",0.0)
> ("population",-2.4649678888894886e-2)
> ("longitude",-4.5966615119112986e-2)
> ("latitude",-0.14416027687448565)

The correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to 1. When it is close to 1, it means there is a strong positive correlation: for example, the median house value tends to go up when the median income goes up. When it is close to -1, there is a strong negative correlation (you can see a small one between the latitude and the median house value, prices have a slight tendency to go down as you go north). Coefficients close to 0 mean there is no linear correlation. (`ocean_proximity` shows 0.0 only because it is text, so Pearson's r is undefined for it.)

The coefficient only measures linear correlations, it may completely miss nonlinear relationships. The most promising attribute to predict the median house value is the median income, so let's zoom in on their scatterplot:

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import Granite.Data.Frame
import Granite.Render.Pipeline
import Granite.Spec
import qualified Data.Text as T

incomeFrame =
    fromColumns
        [ ("income", ColNum (D.columnAsList median_income df))
        , ("value", ColNum (D.columnAsList median_house_value df))
        ]

incomeLayer =
    (defLayer GeomPoint)
        { layerMapping =
            emptyMapping
                { aesX = Just (ColumnRef "income")
                , aesY = Just (ColumnRef "value")
                }
        , layerAesDef = emptyAesDefaults{defSize = Just 2, defAlpha = Just 0.1}
        }

incomeChart =
    emptyChart
        { chartData = incomeFrame
        , chartLayers = [incomeLayer]
        , chartTitle = Just "Median income vs median house value"
        , chartSize = SizePixels 760 560
        }

displayHtml (T.unpack (renderChartSvg incomeChart))
```

## Experimenting with attribute combinations
One last thing you may want to do before preparing the data for machine learning is to try out various attribute combinations. The total number of rooms in a district is not very useful if you don't know how many households there are. What you really want is the number of rooms per household. Similarly, the total number of bedrooms by itself is not very useful: you probably want to compare it to the number of rooms. And the population per household also seems like an interesting combination to look at. Let's create these new attributes (imputing the missing `total_bedrooms` values with the column median so the ratio is defined everywhere):

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import DataFrame.Operators
import Data.Function (on)
import qualified Data.List as L
import Data.Maybe (fromMaybe)

bedroomsMedian = D.medianMaybe total_bedrooms df
imputedBedrooms = F.fromMaybe bedroomsMedian total_bedrooms

withCombos =
    df
        |> D.derive "rooms_per_household" (total_rooms / households)
        |> D.derive "bedrooms_per_room" (imputedBedrooms / total_rooms)
        |> D.derive "population_per_household" (population / households)

corrAug name = (name, fromMaybe 0 (D.correlation name "median_house_value" withCombos))

mapM_ print (L.sortBy (flip compare `on` snd) (map corrAug (D.columnNames withCombos)))
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> ("median_house_value",1.0)
> ("median_income",0.6880752079585185)
> ("rooms_per_household",0.1519482897414869)
> ("total_rooms",0.13415311380656322)
> ("housing_median_age",0.10562341249320993)
> ("households",6.584265057005642e-2)
> ("total_bedrooms",4.914821959942548e-2)
> ("ocean_proximity",0.0)
> ("population_per_household",-2.373741295613557e-2)
> ("population",-2.4649678888894886e-2)
> ("longitude",-4.5966615119112986e-2)
> ("latitude",-0.14416027687448565)
> ("bedrooms_per_room",-0.23330292651591122)

Not bad! The new `bedrooms_per_room` attribute is much more correlated with the median house value than the total number of rooms or bedrooms. Apparently houses with a lower bedroom/room ratio tend to be more expensive. The number of rooms per household is also more informative than the total number of rooms in a district, obviously the larger the houses, the more expensive they are.

(Our `bedrooms_per_room` correlation is a touch weaker than the book's -0.26 because we imputed the missing bedroom counts with the median rather than dropping those rows; the conclusion is the same.)

This round of exploration does not have to be absolutely thorough; the point is to start off on the right foot and quickly gain insights that will help you get a first reasonably good prototype. But this is an iterative process: once you have a prototype up and running, you can analyse its output to gain more insights and come back to this step.

<!-- sabela:cell -->

## Prepare the data for Machine Learning algorithms
It's time to prepare the data for our machine learning algorithms. Instead of doing this manually, we write functions, for several good reasons:

- This lets us reproduce these transformations easily on any dataset (for example the next time we get a fresh dataset).
- We gradually build a library of transformation functions we can reuse in future projects.
- We can use these functions in the live system to transform new data before feeding it to the algorithms.

Let's work from the stratified training set, dropping the `income_cat` helper column we used for sampling. We keep the predictors and the labels apart, since we don't want to apply the same transformations to the predictors and the target values.
```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import DataFrame.Operators
import System.Random (mkStdGen)

-- stratifiedSplit returns the (ratio-fraction, remainder) pair, so with 0.2
-- the first element is the ~20% test portion and the second is the ~80% train.
(stratTestSet, stratTrainSet) =
    D.stratifiedSplit (mkStdGen 42) 0.2 (F.col @Int "income_cat") dfWithIncomeCat

-- the training set, without the income_cat helper column
housing = stratTrainSet |> D.exclude ["income_cat"]

-- keep predictors and labels apart: we never transform the target
housingLabels = D.columnAsList median_house_value housing

(D.dimensions stratTestSet, D.dimensions stratTrainSet, D.dimensions housing)
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> ((4080,11),(16560,11),(16560,10))

### Data cleaning and feature engineering
Most machine learning algorithms cannot work with missing features. The `total_bedrooms` attribute has some gaps, so we fill them with the **training** median (and keep that median so the test set and any future data are filled the same way). In the same pass we engineer the ratio features we found useful during exploration (rooms per household, bedrooms per room, population per household) and ordinal-encode `ocean_proximity`.

We do this with dataframe's monadic API (`FrameM`), which threads the frame through each step for us: `imputeM` hands back the filled column as an expression we reuse for the bedroom ratio, and the typed column references generated above mean there is not a single hand-written `F.col @Type "name"` to get wrong.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import DataFrame.Operators
import DataFrame.Monad

-- ordinal encoding for the one categorical column, ordered by distance to the ocean
ordinalOcean :: Text -> Double
ordinalOcean op = case op of
    "ISLAND" -> 5
    "NEAR OCEAN" -> 4
    "NEAR BAY" -> 3
    "<1H OCEAN" -> 2
    "INLAND" -> 1
    _ -> 0

(trainBedroomsMedian, housingFeatured) = runFrameM housing $ do
    medBeds <- inspectM (D.medianMaybe total_bedrooms)
    bedrooms <- imputeM total_bedrooms medBeds
    _ <- deriveM "rooms_per_household" (total_rooms / households)
    _ <- deriveM "bedrooms_per_room" (bedrooms / total_rooms)
    _ <- deriveM "population_per_household" (population / households)
    _ <- deriveM "ocean_proximity" (F.lift ordinalOcean ocean_proximity)
    pure medBeds

housingFeatured
    |> D.take 5
    |> D.select ["total_bedrooms", "rooms_per_household", "bedrooms_per_room", "population_per_household", "ocean_proximity"]
    |> D.toMarkdown'
    |> displayMarkdown
```

### Feature scaling
One of the most important transformations you need to apply to your data is feature scaling. With few exceptions, machine learning algorithms don't perform well when the input numerical attributes have very different scales: the total number of rooms ranges from about 6 to 39,320, while the median income only ranges from 0 to 15.

There are two common ways to get all attributes to the same scale: min-max scaling (normalization) and standardization. Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so each feature ends up with zero mean and unit variance; it is much less affected by outliers than min-max scaling. We use standardization here, fitting the mean and standard deviation on the training set only (and the target, `median_house_value`, is left untouched).

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import DataFrame.Operators

-- every numeric feature column: select all Double columns, drop the target
doubleFeatures =
    housingFeatured
        |> D.selectBy [D.byProperty (D.hasElemType @Double)]
        |> D.exclude ["median_house_value"]
featureColumns = D.columnNames doubleFeatures

-- per-feature mean and standard deviation, fitted on the training set
trainStats =
    [ (name, D.mean (F.col @Double name) housingFeatured, D.standardDeviation (F.col @Double name) housingFeatured)
    | name <- featureColumns
    ]

standardizeWith stats d =
    foldl (\acc (name, m, s) -> D.derive name ((F.col @Double name - F.lit m) / F.lit s) acc) d stats

housingScaled = standardizeWith trainStats housingFeatured

housingScaled |> D.summarize |> D.toMarkdown' |> displayMarkdown
```

### Transformation pipeline
There are many data transformation steps that need to run in the right order. Scikit-learn provides a `Pipeline` class for this; in Haskell a pipeline is just function composition, chaining the steps with `|>`. We package the whole sequence (impute, combine attributes, encode the category, standardise) into a single `prepare` function, fitted on the training set, that we can apply to the test set and to new data later. As a sanity check, re-preparing the training set reproduces the scaled frame we built step by step above.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import DataFrame.Monad

-- the full preparation, fitted on the training set and reusable on any raw frame
-- (the test set, new data): impute with the training median, engineer the ratio
-- features, encode the category, then standardise with the training statistics.
prepareFrame :: D.DataFrame -> D.DataFrame
prepareFrame raw = standardizeWith trainStats engineered
  where
    engineered = execFrameM raw $ do
        bedrooms <- imputeM total_bedrooms trainBedroomsMedian
        _ <- deriveM "rooms_per_household" (total_rooms / households)
        _ <- deriveM "bedrooms_per_room" (bedrooms / total_rooms)
        _ <- deriveM "population_per_household" (population / households)
        _ <- deriveM "ocean_proximity" (F.lift ordinalOcean ocean_proximity)
        pure ()

(D.dimensions (prepareFrame housing), D.dimensions housingScaled)
```

> ((16560,13),(16560,13))

## Select and train a model
At last! You framed the problem, got the data and explored it, sampled a training set and a test set, and wrote a preparation pipeline to clean up and prepare the data automatically. You are now ready to select and train a model.

In `dataframe-learn` every estimator speaks two verbs: `fit` trains a model from a config and a target column, and `predict` hands back an `Expr` over the columns that you drop straight into `derive` (a fitted model literally is a dataframe expression you can read and apply). Let's first train a linear regression model, ordinary least squares, configured by `defaultLinearConfig`.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import DataFrame.Operators
import DataFrame.LinearModel
import DataFrame.Model (fit, predict)

-- fit OLS using the typed target reference; predict compiles to an Expr we derive
linModel = fit defaultLinearConfig median_house_value housingScaled
linScored = D.derive "linear_pred" (predict linModel) housingScaled

putStrLn (D.prettyPrint (predict linModel))

linScored |> D.select ["median_house_value", "linear_pred"] |> D.take 5 |> D.toMarkdown' |> displayMarkdown
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F

-- root mean squared error of a prediction column against the target
rmseOf predCol d =
    let ps = D.columnAsList (F.col @Double predCol) d
        as = D.columnAsList median_house_value d
     in sqrt (sum [(p - a) * (p - a) | (p, a) <- zip ps as] / fromIntegral (length ps))

linRmse = rmseOf "linear_pred" linScored
linRmse
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> 68487.96506393426

This is better than nothing, but clearly not a great score: most districts' median house values range between about $120,000 and $265,000, so a typical prediction error of around $68,000 is not very satisfying. This is a textbook case of a model underfitting the training data. When this happens it can mean the features don't provide enough information, or the model isn't powerful enough. Let's try a more powerful model: a decision tree, which can find complex nonlinear relationships in the data.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import DataFrame.Operators
import DataFrame.DecisionTree.Regression (defaultRegTreeConfig, RegTreeConfig (..))
import DataFrame.DecisionTree.Model ()
import DataFrame.Model (fit, predict)

-- let the tree grow fully so it can (over)fit the training data
treeConfig = defaultRegTreeConfig{rtMaxDepth = 30, rtMinSamplesSplit = 2, rtMinLeafSize = 1}
treeModel = fit treeConfig median_house_value housingScaled
treeScored = D.derive "tree_pred" (predict treeModel) housingScaled

treeRmse = rmseOf "tree_pred" treeScored
treeRmse
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> 726.1204676045394

```haskell
-- cabal: build-depends: dataframe-core
import DataFrame.Internal.Expression (eSize)

eSize (predict treeModel)
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> 78791

Wait, an RMSE of around 700? Almost no error at all. And our tree has 78'000 nodes? It is far more likely that the model has badly overfit the training data than that it is nearly perfect. How can we be sure? We don't want to touch the test set until we are confident in a model, so we use part of the training set for training and part for validation.

A great way to do this is K-fold cross-validation: randomly split the training set into K folds, then train and evaluate the model K times, each time holding out a different fold for validation and training on the other K-1. The result is K evaluation scores.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import DataFrame.Operators
import DataFrame.DecisionTree.Model ()
import DataFrame.Model (fit, predict)
import System.Random (mkStdGen)

meanD xs = sum xs / fromIntegral (length xs)
stdD xs = let m = meanD xs in sqrt (meanD [(x - m) * (x - m) | x <- xs])

-- K-fold cross-validation RMSE for any "train a frame -> prediction Expr" function
crossValRmse :: Int -> (D.DataFrame -> D.Expr Double) -> D.DataFrame -> [Double]
crossValRmse k trainPredictor d =
    let shuffled = D.shuffle (mkStdGen 42) d
        withFold = D.insert "cv_fold" (map (`mod` k) [0 .. D.nRows shuffled - 1]) shuffled
        foldRmse i =
            let train = withFold |> D.filter (F.col @Int "cv_fold") (/= i) |> D.exclude ["cv_fold"]
                test = withFold |> D.filter (F.col @Int "cv_fold") (== i) |> D.exclude ["cv_fold"]
                scored = D.derive "cv_pred" (trainPredictor train) test
             in rmseOf "cv_pred" scored
     in map foldRmse [0 .. k - 1]

treeCvScores = crossValRmse 5 (\tr -> predict (fit treeConfig median_house_value tr)) housingScaled

putStrLn ("Decision tree, 5-fold CV RMSE: mean " ++ show (round (meanD treeCvScores) :: Int) ++ " +/- " ++ show (round (stdD treeCvScores) :: Int))
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> Decision tree, 5-fold CV RMSE: mean 69183 +/- 1492

Now the decision tree doesn't look so good: a cross-validated RMSE around 69,000, far worse than its ~700 training error. Cross-validation gives us not just an estimate of performance but a sense of how precise it is (the standard deviation). Let's compute the same scores for the linear regression model to compare:

```haskell
import DataFrame.LinearModel
import DataFrame.Model (fit, predict)

linCvScores = crossValRmse 5 (\tr -> predict (fit defaultLinearConfig median_house_value tr)) housingScaled

putStrLn ("Linear regression, 5-fold CV RMSE: mean " ++ show (round (meanD linCvScores) :: Int) ++ " +/- " ++ show (round (stdD linCvScores) :: Int))
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> Linear regression, 5-fold CV RMSE: mean 68711 +/- 1304

The decision tree performs about the same as linear regression, sometimes a touch worse: it overfits so badly that, once cross-validated, it gives up its apparent advantage. Let's try one last model: a random forest, which trains many decision trees on random subsets of the data and averages their predictions. Building a model on top of many other models is called ensemble learning, and it is often a great way to push performance further. `dataframe-learn` has no forest of its own, so we bag the regression tree ourselves: train each tree on a bootstrap sample (rows drawn with replacement) and average the resulting prediction expressions.

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F
import DataFrame.Operations.Subset (selectRows)
import DataFrame.DecisionTree.Regression (defaultRegTreeConfig, RegTreeConfig (..))
import DataFrame.DecisionTree.Model ()
import DataFrame.Model (fit, predict)
import System.Random (mkStdGen, randomRs)

forestConfig = defaultRegTreeConfig{rtMaxDepth = 12, rtMinSamplesSplit = 2, rtMinLeafSize = 1}
nTrees = 6
sampleSize = 8000

-- a bootstrap sample of sampleSize rows drawn with replacement
bootstrapSample seed d = selectRows (take sampleSize (randomRs (0, D.nRows d - 1) (mkStdGen seed))) d

-- average the predictions of nTrees trees, each trained on its own bootstrap sample
forestPredictorOn d =
    foldr1 (+) [predict (fit forestConfig median_house_value (bootstrapSample s d)) | s <- [1 .. nTrees]]
        / F.lit (fromIntegral nTrees)

forestScored = D.derive "forest_pred" (forestPredictorOn housingScaled) housingScaled
forestRmse = rmseOf "forest_pred" forestScored
forestRmse
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> 41990.714560590495

Much better: the bagged forest reaches a training RMSE far below linear regression or the single tree, and averaging across trees tames the wild overfitting we saw from one tree. It is the most promising of our three models. (This is still the training error, though, so the score on the test set will be higher.)

There is no more hyperparameter tuning to labour here, so let's take the forest as our final model and see how it does on the test set we put aside at the very beginning.

<!-- sabela:cell -->

## Evaluate your system on the test set
After tweaking the models for a while, we finally have a system that performs reasonably well. Now is the time to evaluate the final model on the test set. There is nothing special about this: we prepare the test set with the **same** pipeline (transforming it with the statistics fitted on the training set, never refitting), train the forest on the full training set, and measure its RMSE on the test set.
```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D

-- prepare the held-out test set with the training-fitted pipeline (no refit)
testPrepared = prepareFrame (D.exclude ["income_cat"] stratTestSet)

-- the final model: the bagged forest trained on the full training set
finalForest = forestPredictorOn housingScaled

testScored = D.derive "forest_pred" finalForest testPrepared
finalRmse = rmseOf "forest_pred" testScored
finalRmse
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> 54224.27757094965

```haskell
import qualified DataFrame as D
import qualified DataFrame.Functions as F

-- a 95% confidence interval for the generalization RMSE, from the spread of the
-- per-district squared errors (normal approximation; the test set is large)
testPreds = D.columnAsList (F.col @Double "forest_pred") testScored
testActs = D.columnAsList median_house_value testScored
sqErrs = [(p - a) * (p - a) | (p, a) <- zip testPreds testActs]
nTest = length sqErrs
meanSq = sum sqErrs / fromIntegral nTest
seSq = sqrt (sum [(e - meanSq) * (e - meanSq) | e <- sqErrs] / fromIntegral (nTest - 1)) / sqrt (fromIntegral nTest)

putStrLn ("95% confidence interval for the test RMSE: [" ++ show (round (sqrt (meanSq - 1.96 * seSq)) :: Int) ++ ", " ++ show (round (sqrt (meanSq + 1.96 * seSq)) :: Int) ++ "]")
```

> <!-- scripths:mime text/plain -->
> 95% confidence interval for the test RMSE: [51830, 56518]

A point estimate of the generalization error is often not enough; the confidence interval shows how precise it is. If you did a lot of hyperparameter tuning, the test score is usually a little worse than what cross-validation suggested, because the system ends up fine-tuned to the validation data. When that happens, resist the temptation to tweak the hyperparameters to make the test number look good: those improvements would not generalise to new data.

## Launch, monitor, and maintain your system
Now comes the prelaunch phase: present your solution (what you learned, what worked and what did not, the assumptions you made, and your system's limitations), document everything, and create clear visualisations. Then get the model ready for production: save the trained pipeline (here that is `prepareFrame` together with the fitted forest), load it in the production environment, and serve predictions through it. Write monitoring code to check the live performance at regular intervals and raise an alert when it drops, because models tend to rot over time as the world changes. Automate collecting fresh data, retraining, and evaluating each new version against the one in production before promoting it.

That is the project end to end. As you have seen, most of the work is in framing the problem, preparing the data, and building a clean, reusable pipeline; the learning algorithms themselves are a comparatively small part.
